questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Magnitude of a vector from its three components
questions.learningObjective: compute the magnitude of a three dimensional vector from its components
questions.practice: reading the magnitude off the components of a vector
questions.stem: A vector in three dimensions has components 3, 4 and 12. Which statement about its magnitude is correct?

options.text: It is the square root of the sum of the squares of the three components
It is the sum of the absolute values of the three components
options.misconception: adds the components in place of combining their squares

options.text: It is the product of the three components taken together
options.misconception: multiplies the components instead of combining their squares

options.text: It is the largest component minus the smallest component
options.misconception: takes a range across the components rather than a norm

questions.explanation: The magnitude of a vector is the norm of its component list, which is the square root of the sum of the squares: the square root of 9 plus 16 plus 144 is the square root of 169, which is 13. Adding the components gives 19, which is the taxicab distance along the edges of a box and is not the straight line length, while multiplying them has no geometric meaning at all. The trap worth naming is the range: the largest component minus the smallest measures spread, not size, and it is not even invariant under a rigid motion.
questions.hint: Square each component and add the results before taking the root.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Constructing a unit vector by rescaling
questions.learningObjective: justify dividing a vector by its magnitude to obtain a unit vector
questions.practice: explaining the normalisation step
questions.stem: Why is the unit vector in the direction of a obtained by dividing a by its magnitude?

options.text: Division rescales the vector to length exactly one while leaving its direction unchanged
Division reverses the direction so the result points along the positive axes
options.misconception: believes normalisation flips a vector toward the positive octant

options.text: Division rounds each component to the nearest integer for convenient arithmetic
options.misconception: believes the quotient is rounded to whole numbers as a side effect

options.text: Division is only a legal operation when the magnitude is already equal to one
options.misconception: thinks division by a length is undefined unless the length is one

questions.explanation: Scaling a vector by any positive number leaves the direction untouched and multiplies the length by that same number, so dividing by the magnitude forces the length to one and does nothing else. That is exactly what a unit vector is asked for: a representative of the direction alone, with the size stripped away. The tempting alternative is to round, on the grounds that a direction is easier to remember in whole numbers, but rounding destroys the very property being asked for and makes the result useless inside a dot product, where lengths matter.
questions.hint: Ask what dividing by a length does to the length, and what it does to the direction.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Orthogonality read off a dot product
questions.learningObjective: recognise perpendicularity from a zero dot product
questions.practice: reading angle information off a dot product
questions.stem: Two nonzero vectors u and v have a dot product of 0. What does that tell you about them?

options.text: They are perpendicular, since only a right angle makes the dot product vanish
They have equal magnitude, since a zero product suggests equal size
options.misconception: reads a zero dot product as a statement about length rather than angle

options.text: The sum u plus v is the zero vector, since a zero product means cancellation
options.misconception: believes a zero dot product means the vectors are opposites

options.text: The projection of u onto v is zero, so u must lie inside the plane of v
options.misconception: confuses a zero dot product with a zero projection component

questions.explanation: The dot product equals the product of the two magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them, and the only angle whose cosine is zero is a right angle. So a zero dot product with both vectors nonzero is precisely the statement that the two directions are perpendicular. The common misreading treats the dot product as a measure of size, but it is a measure of orientation: two vectors of very different lengths meeting at a right angle still give zero, and two vectors of identical length pointing the same way give a large positive number.
questions.hint: Write the dot product as the product of two magnitudes times a cosine.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Sign of a dot product and the angle it reveals
questions.learningObjective: relate the sign of a dot product to the angle between two vectors
questions.practice: classifying an angle from a dot product sign
questions.stem: If the dot product of two nonzero vectors is positive, what is true of the angle between them?

options.text: The angle is less than ninety degrees, so the vectors point broadly the same way
The angle is more than ninety degrees, so the vectors point broadly apart
options.misconception: reverses the sign convention between a positive product and an obtuse angle

options.text: The angle is exactly ninety degrees, so the vectors are strictly perpendicular
options.misconception: takes every zero cosine as applying to any nonzero product as well

options.text: The angle is a full half turn, so one vector is the negative of the other
options.misconception: confuses a negative dot product with the most negative one possible

questions.explanation: Since the product of the magnitudes is positive for nonzero vectors, the sign of the dot product is the sign of the cosine, and a positive cosine means an acute angle. The three failure modes are the three other regimes of the cosine: negative gives an obtuse angle, exactly zero gives a right angle, and the extreme negative value of minus one gives the half turn in which one vector is the negative of the other. Deciding between them is a matter of tracking the sign, not the size of the number.
questions.hint: Track the sign of the cosine, not the size of the dot product.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: The right hand rule fixes the direction of a cross product
questions.learningObjective: state what determines the direction of a cross product
questions.practice: justifying the orientation of a cross product
questions.stem: The cross product of a and b is perpendicular to both of them. Which fact fixes which of the two perpendicular directions it points?

options.text: The right hand rule, curling the fingers from a towards b and reading along the thumb
The rule that the first two entries of the result are built from the pairs in order
options.misconception: believes a fixed slot order in the formula settles the orientation

options.text: The convention that the larger of the two entries of the result is taken positive
options.misconception: believes a sign chosen by size replaces a genuine orientation convention

options.text: Nothing fixes it, because the two perpendicular directions are equally valid
options.misconception: believes the cross product is only determined up to sign by the algebra

questions.explanation: The algebra fixes a direction, not merely a line, but only once an orientation convention is supplied, and the right hand rule is that convention: point the fingers along a, curl them towards b, and the thumb gives the direction of the result. Reversing the order of the two inputs reverses the result, which is the clearest evidence that a convention and not the components alone is at work. A slot order in the formula only says where each entry is written down; it cannot by itself tell you which of the two perpendicular directions is meant.
questions.hint: Ask what the formula leaves undetermined, and what a convention supplies.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Geometric meaning of the magnitude of a cross product
questions.learningObjective: identify the quantity measured by a cross product magnitude
questions.practice: matching a cross product magnitude to an area
questions.stem: What does the magnitude of the cross product of a and b measure?

options.text: The area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b, which the two vectors bound
The area of the triangle spanned by a and b, which is half that parallelogram
options.misconception: halves the parallelogram area and so forgets the second triangle

options.text: The volume of the box spanned by a, b and their own cross product together
options.misconception: confuses the two dimensional result with a three dimensional one

options.text: The product of the two magnitudes, which equals the area only when they are square
options.misconception: drops the sine factor and so confuses area with the enclosing rectangle

questions.explanation: The magnitude of a cross product is the product of the two magnitudes times the sine of the angle between them, and that is exactly the area of the parallelogram with those two vectors as adjacent sides. Since a triangle drawn on the same two sides has half that area, the triangle reading is off by a factor of two. The other confusion is dropping the sine: the product of the magnitudes is the area of the enclosing rectangle, reached only when the vectors happen to meet at a right angle.
questions.hint: Compare the product of two magnitudes times a sine with an area on a diagram.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: What determines a plane in three dimensions
questions.learningObjective: identify the data that pin down a plane in space
questions.practice: choosing data that determine a plane
questions.stem: What data determine a plane in three dimensions?

options.text: Three non-collinear points, or equivalently one point with two non-parallel directions
Two distinct points, since the line through them must lie inside the plane
options.misconception: believes a line is enough to pin down a plane in space

options.text: One point together with one direction vector, which fixes a line but not a plane
options.misconception: believes point plus one direction is a complete plane description

options.text: Three points that happen to be collinear, since a line is a special kind of plane
options.misconception: believes collinear points still determine a plane because three is the right count

questions.explanation: A plane is a two dimensional object, so it takes one point to say where it is and two independent directions to say how it is tilted, and two directions are exactly what two non-parallel vectors in the plane supply. Three non-collinear points encode the same information, since two of the three differences between them give the two directions. Either of the last two choices leaves one degree of freedom free: a line in space can sit in infinitely many planes, and a single point plus a single direction likewise describes only a line, so the data do not determine a unique plane.
questions.hint: Count the degrees of freedom a plane has, and match them to the data given.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: What a normal vector to a plane is good for
questions.learningObjective: state the role of a normal vector to a plane
questions.practice: justifying the use of a normal vector
questions.stem: Why is a normal vector to a plane worth computing?

options.text: It is perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane, which turns distance into a dot product
It lies inside the plane, so it can be added to any direction that also lies there
options.misconception: believes the normal is a direction in the plane rather than across it

options.text: It is parallel to every line that meets the plane, so it names the whole family
options.misconception: believes meeting a plane forces a line to follow the normal direction

options.text: Its length equals the area of the plane, so it measures the plane's size directly
options.misconception: believes the length of a normal carries the size of the plane

questions.explanation: A normal is perpendicular to the whole plane, so it is perpendicular to every direction lying in it, and that single fact is what makes distance computable: the distance from a point to the plane is a dot product of the displacement with the unit normal, divided by nothing further. Nothing about the normal is inside the plane, and nothing forces lines meeting the plane to follow it, since a line can meet a plane at any angle at all. Its length is a free choice of scaling, so it cannot encode the size of the plane.
questions.hint: Ask what perpendicularity buys you, in particular for computing a distance.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: What determines a line in three dimensions
questions.learningObjective: identify the data that pin down a line in space
questions.practice: choosing data that determine a line
questions.stem: What data determine a line in three dimensions?

options.text: One point on the line together with one direction vector that is not the zero vector
Three points on the line, which fix a direction more tightly than a single point does
options.misconception: believes three collinear points are needed to fix a direction

options.text: One direction vector on its own, with no point, since a direction names a family
options.misconception: believes a direction alone determines a single line rather than a family

options.text: One plane that contains the line, since any plane fixes every direction within it
options.misconception: believes a containing plane determines a line inside it

questions.explanation: A line is a one dimensional object, so it takes one point to say where it is and one nonzero direction to say which way it runs, and those two pieces are exactly the standard description. The reason the other three fail is that each of them leaves a degree of freedom unfixed. A direction with no point names the family of all parallel lines, a plane contains infinitely many lines, and extra collinear points on a line that is already determined add nothing at all.
questions.hint: A line has one degree of freedom for position and one for direction.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Two non-parallel lines in a plane meet at one point
questions.learningObjective: state how many points two non-parallel lines in a plane share
questions.practice: reasoning about how two lines in a plane can meet
questions.stem: Two lines in the same plane are distinct and are not parallel. What must be true of them?

options.text: They share exactly one point, which fixes a value of each line's parameter
They share two points, one on each side of the plane that holds them both
options.misconception: believes a pair of lines in a plane can cross twice

options.text: They share no point, because two lines in a plane always stay apart
options.misconception: believes two lines in a plane cannot cross at all

options.text: They share a whole segment, since both lines extend without bound in both ways
options.misconception: believes overlapping lines still count as distinct

questions.explanation: Two lines in one plane either have the same direction, in which case they are parallel and never meet, or they have different directions, in which case following each one far enough makes the separation grow without bound in both directions, so they must cross exactly once. The crossing point is what pins down one value of each line's parameter, which is why a system of two linear equations in two unknowns is exactly the right shape for the problem. The other three options describe situations that the definition of a line in a plane rules out.
questions.hint: Two different directions in a plane cannot stay a positive distance apart.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: A plane angle is the complement of the angle between normals
questions.learningObjective: relate the angle between two planes to the angle between their normals
questions.practice: converting between plane angles and normal angles
questions.stem: How is the angle a plane makes with a coordinate plane related to the angles of the two normal vectors?

options.text: It is the complement of the angle between the two normal vectors
It is the angle between the two normal vectors, with no change made
options.misconception: believes the two angles are equal rather than complementary

options.text: It is the angle between one normal and a line in the coordinate plane
options.misconception: measures against a direction lying in the plane instead of a normal

options.text: It is the angle swept by turning the plane straight onto the other one
options.misconception: restates the plane angle without relating it to any normals

questions.explanation: Each normal is perpendicular to its own plane, so tipping one plane onto the other carries its normal through the same tilt, and the two normals are then separated by a right angle less that tilt. The plane angle is the tilt and the normal angle is what remains of the right angle, so the two always add to ninety degrees. The limiting cases show it: a plane coinciding with the coordinate plane has parallel normals and a plane angle of ninety degrees, while a plane standing perpendicular to it has a normal lying inside the coordinate plane and a plane angle of zero.
questions.hint: Watch what happens to the two normals as one plane tips onto the other.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: What a projection keeps and what it discards
questions.learningObjective: describe what a projection retains and what it removes
questions.practice: describing a projection geometrically
questions.stem: What does the vector projection of a onto b keep from the vector a?

options.text: The part of a that lies along b, and nothing of the part across b
The part of a that lies across b, and nothing of the part along b
options.misconception: keeps the perpendicular component and discards the parallel one

options.text: All of a, since a projection rewrites a without ever removing length
options.misconception: believes a projection preserves the whole vector

options.text: The sum of a and b, since a projection folds two vectors into one result
options.misconception: believes a projection adds the two inputs together

questions.explanation: Any vector splits uniquely into a piece parallel to b and a piece perpendicular to b, and the projection is exactly the parallel piece, so it keeps the part of a that lies along b and discards the part that lies across it. The two pieces are orthogonal, so the magnitude of a is the square root of the sum of their squared lengths, which is Pythagoras rather than addition; adding the pieces would be wrong precisely because they meet at a right angle. The scalar component is the length of that parallel piece, so it and the vector projection carry the same information in different forms.
questions.hint: Split a into the part along b and the part at right angles to b.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: A triple product measures a volume
questions.learningObjective: identify the quantity measured by a scalar triple product
questions.practice: matching a triple product to a volume
questions.stem: What does the absolute value of the scalar triple product of three vectors measure?

options.text: The volume of the parallelepiped that the three vectors span
The area of the parallelogram spanned by the last two of the three vectors
options.misconception: reports a two dimensional quantity from a three dimensional construction

options.text: The volume of the tetrahedron whose three edges are those same vectors
options.misconception: reports the sixth of the volume rather than the volume

options.text: The product of the three magnitudes, which ignores the angles between them
options.misconception: drops every angle, so the vectors could fail to span a box at all

questions.explanation: The cross product of the first two vectors gives the area of the parallelogram they span, along a direction perpendicular to it, and dotting that with the third vector projects the third onto that normal, supplying the height. Area times height is the volume of the parallelepiped, so the absolute value of the triple product is that volume, with the sign discarded because geometry does not record an orientation. The tetrahedron on the same three edges is one sixth of the same number, and the bare product of the magnitudes would be the volume of a box with the three edge lengths but ignoring every angle, which is generally larger.
questions.hint: Take the cross product first, then ask what the dot product with the third vector adds.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why transformations need a homogeneous coordinate
questions.learningObjective: state what the extra homogeneous coordinate makes possible
questions.practice: justifying the use of a fourth coordinate
questions.stem: Why is a fourth coordinate added when points are moved around by a transformation matrix?

options.text: It lets a scaling that depends on the point, such as perspective, reach the answer
It stores four numbers where the geometry of space only ever needs three
options.misconception: believes the fourth coordinate carries extra geometric information

options.text: It removes the need for a translation, which is the hardest move to express
options.misconception: believes the fourth coordinate makes translation unnecessary

options.text: It guarantees that every such matrix preserves lengths and angles exactly
options.misconception: believes adding a coordinate makes any matrix a rigid motion

questions.explanation: A three by three matrix has three output coordinates, and a linear map with no translation has to send multiples of a direction to multiples of the same direction with one fixed multiple for every direction. Perspective needs the multiple to vary from point to point, since the amount of compression depends on how far the point sits from the eye, and three coordinates have no room to record that. A fourth coordinate, free to differ between points, carries the scale, and dividing the first three by it at the end performs the projection. The fourth number is bookkeeping rather than geometry, and it also absorbs translation into the same matrix, but it does not make every matrix length-preserving.
questions.hint: Ask what a matrix with three output rows cannot record about each point.

questions.learningObjective: compute a vector magnitude from three components
questions.practice: square root of a sum of three squares
questions.stem: What is the magnitude of the vector whose components are 3, 4 and 12?
questions.explanation: Square each component and add: 9 plus 16 plus 144 is 169. The magnitude is the square root of that, which is 13. The traps are adding the components for 19, which is the path along the edges of a box rather than the straight line, and halving the sum of squares, which has no justification at all.

questions.topic: Third component of a unit vector
questions.learningObjective: normalise a vector and read off one component
questions.practice: building a unit vector and extracting a component
questions.stem: A vector has components 2, 3 and 6. What is the third component of the unit vector pointing in its direction?
questions.explanation: The magnitude is the square root of 4 plus 9 plus 36, which is the square root of 49, so it is 7. Dividing the third component 6 by 7 gives 0.857143. Leaving the component as 6 forgets the normalisation entirely, and dividing by the number of components or by 6 itself are both ways of misreading what the denominator is for.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Dot product of two three dimensional vectors
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a dot product componentwise
questions.practice: multiplying and summing matching components
questions.stem: What is the dot product of the vector (1, 2, 3) with the vector (4, -5, 6)?
questions.explanation: Multiply matching components and add: 1 times 4 is 4, 2 times minus 5 is minus 10, and 3 times 6 is 18, and 4 minus 10 plus 18 is 12. Skipping the middle term, which is the usual slip, gives 22, and taking absolute values throughout gives 32; both discard information the definition requires.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Angle between two vectors from a dot product
questions.learningObjective: recover the angle between two vectors from their dot product and magnitudes
questions.practice: inverting the dot product formula for the angle
questions.stem: In degrees, what is the angle between the vector (1, 2, 3) and the vector (4, -5, 6)?
questions.explanation: The magnitudes are the square root of 14 and the square root of 77, and the dot product is 12, so the cosine of the angle is 12 divided by the square root of 14 times 77, which is 0.3654869. The arccosine of that is 68.5624 degrees. Omitting the magnitude in the denominator forces the cosine above 1 and yields no angle at all, while using the sum of the magnitudes instead of their product is a subtler version of the same slip.
questions.hint: Take the dot product of the cross product of the first two with the third.

questions.topic: Magnitude of a cross product
questions.learningObjective: compute the magnitude of a cross product from its components
questions.practice: magnitude of a cross product and its area meaning
questions.stem: What is the magnitude of the cross product of (1, 2, 3) with (4, -5, 6)?
questions.explanation: The cross product is (27, 6, -13), so its magnitude is the square root of 729 plus 36 plus 169, which is the square root of 934, giving 30.5614. The independent check is the area reading: the two magnitudes are the square root of 14 and the square root of 77 and the sine of the angle is 0.9308, whose product is the same number. Halving this to report a triangle area, or doubling it by forgetting that the sine already appears, are the two slips to avoid.

questions.topic: Area of a triangle from a cross product
questions.learningObjective: obtain the area of a triangle from the cross product of its two sides
questions.practice: half of a parallelogram area
questions.stem: Two vectors have components (1, 0, 2) and (0, 3, 0). What is the area of the triangle that they span from a common vertex?
questions.explanation: The cross product is (-6, 0, 3), whose magnitude is the square root of 36 plus 9, that is 6.7082. That is the area of the parallelogram, and the triangle cut from it by the diagonal is exactly half, giving 3.3541. The independent check is half the product of the two magnitudes times the sine of the angle between them, and it agrees to the last digit shown.

questions.topic: Scalar component along a unit direction
questions.learningObjective: compute the scalar component of a vector along a given unit direction
questions.practice: dot product with a unit vector
questions.stem: What is the scalar component of the vector (3, 4, 0) along the unit vector (0, 0.6, 0.8)?
questions.explanation: The component along a direction is a dot product, so it is 3 times 0 plus 4 times 0.6 plus 0 times 0.8, which is 2.4. The direction given really is a unit vector, since 0.36 plus 0.64 is 1, so no normalisation is needed. Had it not been a unit vector the same dot product would still be computable but would have to be divided by the magnitude of the direction, and skipping that division is the standard slip.
questions.hint: Multiply matching components, keeping the sign of each product.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Length of a projection onto a direction
questions.learningObjective: find the length of the projection of a vector onto a direction
questions.practice: projecting onto a non-unit direction and rescaling
questions.stem: What is the length of the projection of the vector (1, 2, 2) onto the direction given by (1, 1, 0)?
questions.explanation: The direction (1, 1, 0) has magnitude the square root of 2, so the scalar component along it is the dot product 1 plus 2, which is 3, divided by the square root of 2, giving 2.12132. The vector projection is the direction scaled by 3 over 2, namely (1.5, 1.5, 0), whose length is 2.12132 as well, so the scalar and vector routes agree. The trap is dividing by 2 instead of by the square root of 2, which uses the squared magnitude.
questions.hint: Set the cosine equal to the dot product divided by the product of the magnitudes, then invert.

questions.topic: Scalar triple product
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a scalar triple product
questions.practice: cross product followed by a dot product
questions.stem: What is the scalar triple product of the vectors (1, 2, 3), (4, -5, 6) and (2, 1, 0), in that order?
questions.explanation: The cross product of the first two is (27, 6, -13), and dotting that with (2, 1, 0) gives 54 plus 6 plus 0, which is 60. Two independent routes agree: the same value comes from the three by three determinant with those rows, whether expanded along the first row or summed over all six permutations, and from dotting the first vector with the cross product of the other two, which is the cyclic symmetry of the construction.

questions.topic: Volume of a tetrahedron from three edges
questions.learningObjective: obtain the volume of a tetrahedron from three edges meeting at a vertex
questions.practice: one sixth of a scalar triple product
questions.stem: A tetrahedron has three edges from one vertex given by (1, 2, 3), (4, -5, 6) and (2, 1, 0). What is its volume?
questions.explanation: The scalar triple product of the three edge vectors is 60, which is the volume of the parallelepiped they span. The tetrahedron is cut from that box by cutting off three corner tetrahedra similar to it, each of one sixth the volume, so what remains is one sixth of 60, which is 10. Reporting 60 confuses the enclosing box with the solid, and reporting 20 or 30 comes from cutting off the wrong number of corners.
questions.hint: Use the pairs from the second and third entries, in that order.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Vector projection computed from a unit direction
questions.learningObjective: compute the vector projection of one vector onto a unit direction
questions.practice: scaling a unit direction by a dot product
questions.stem: What is the second component of the projection of the vector (3, 4, 0) onto the unit direction (0, 0.6, 0.8)?
questions.explanation: The projection is the dot product scaled through the whole unit direction, and the dot product is 3 times 0 plus 4 times 0.6 plus 0 times 0.8, which is 2.4. Multiplying that into the second component of the direction gives 2.4 times 0.6, which is 1.44, and the full projection is (0, 1.44, 1.92). reorders the coordinates so that they no longer match the axes

is a sphere, since all three squares appear with plus signs

questions.explanation: A cone is the set of rays from a single point, so its equation must be homogeneous: scaling every coordinate by the same factor has to leave the equation true. In x^2 + y^2 = 9z^2 every term is quadratic, and setting z to zero forces x and y to zero, so the origin lies on the surface and is the only such point, which is the vertex. The 9 in the equation sets the opening, giving a half angle whose tangent is 3, that is 71.5651 degrees. has two signs against one, which splits into two sheets
has two signs against one, which splits into two sheets

reverses the first coordinate, which is a half turn

questions.stem: A student claims the vector (2, -1, 4) is a normal to the plane spanned by (1, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 1). What is the error?

options.text: A normal must run parallel to their cross product (1, -1, 1), and this does not
A normal must lie inside the plane, and this vector is neither spanning one
options.misconception: believes a normal is a direction within the plane

options.text: A normal need only be perpendicular to one spanning vector, as this one is
options.misconception: believes perpendicularity to one direction is enough

options.text: A normal must have unit length, so only the length of this vector is wrong
options.misconception: blames the length of a vector that fails a direction test

questions.explanation: The cross product of the two spanning vectors is (1, -1, 1), and that direction, or any nonzero multiple of it, is the only direction perpendicular to the plane. Dotting the claimed normal with it gives 2 plus 1 plus 4, which is 7, so the vector is far from perpendicular and the claim fails outright. Being perpendicular to a single spanning vector would not be enough even if it held, since a vector can clear one direction inside a plane and still tilt out of it, which is why the test uses the perpendicular direction rather than either spanning vector.
questions.hint: A normal must have zero dot product with every direction lying in the plane.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Diagnosing a translation claim that the matrix contradicts
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a claimed image that the transformation matrix contradicts
questions.practice: checking a claimed image against a matrix
questions.stem: A translation by (5, -2, 1) is claimed to send the point (1, 2, 3) to (5, -2, 1). The matrix with rows (1, 0, 0, 5), (0, 1, 0, -2), (0, 0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 0, 1) applied to (1, 2, 3, 1) gives (6, 0, 4, 1). What is the error?

options.text: The matrix adds the shift to the point, so the image is (6, 0, 4) and not the shift
The matrix replaces the point, so the shift vector itself is the true image
options.misconception: believes a translation overwrites the point with the shift

options.text: The last row forces w to 0, so the image must be divided by a vanishing w
options.misconception: believes the last row of an affine matrix zeroes w

options.text: The matrix turns as well as shifts, so the image is not just the plain sum
options.misconception: believes the identity block in a translation matrix turns the point

questions.explanation: A translation moves a point, it does not replace it, so the image is the point plus the shift, which is (6, 0, 4); the student reported the shift itself as the destination, which is the image of the origin rather than of the point. The last row keeps the fourth coordinate at 1, so no division follows, and the leading identity block means nothing is turned. Two independent checks agree: the displacement from the origin to the image is exactly (5, -2, 1), and translating twice gives the point plus twice the shift.
questions.hint: Multiply the homogeneous column by the matrix and read off the result.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why a cross product magnitude is an area
questions.learningObjective: justify that a cross product magnitude measures a parallelogram area
questions.practice: explaining the area meaning of a cross product
questions.stem: Explain why the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors equals the area of the parallelogram that those two vectors span.

answer.exemplar: Write the magnitude of the cross product as the product of the two magnitudes times the sine of the angle between them, and then look at the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are those two vectors. Drop a perpendicular from the far end of one side onto the line carrying the other: the base is the length of the first vector, the height is the length of the second times the sine of the included angle, and the area of the figure is exactly that product. The cross product magnitude is the same expression, so the two agree by more than coincidence: both come from resolving one side against the direction perpendicular to the other. The direction of the cross product completes the picture, because it is perpendicular to both sides and therefore normal to the parallelogram, so one object carries both pieces of information, the direction of the normal and the size of the area. A worthwhile contrast is the dot product, which multiplies by the cosine instead and so measures a projection rather than an area. The sine and the cosine are exactly what separate the two products geometrically, which is why the same two inputs give one length and one area depending on which is taken.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to connect the algebraic form, the product of the magnitudes times a sine, to the area of the parallelogram built on those two sides, and to say why a sine appears there. It should also note that the direction of the result is normal to that parallelogram, so the one object carries both the normal direction and the area.
questions.hint: Start from the sine formula and picture the parallelogram built on those two sides.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why a triple product is a volume and the tetrahedron is a sixth of it
questions.learningObjective: justify the volume reading of a scalar triple product and the sixth for a tetrahedron
questions.practice: explaining the volume meaning of a triple product
questions.stem: Explain why the absolute value of a scalar triple product is a volume, and why the tetrahedron on the same three edges has one sixth of that volume.

answer.exemplar: Take the first two vectors and form their cross product. Its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram they span, and its direction is perpendicular to both, hence perpendicular to that whole parallelogram. A box has volume equal to base area times perpendicular height, and the third vector supplies exactly that height once projected onto the direction of the cross product, which is the dot product of the third vector with the cross product. The absolute value is taken because a signed volume would record an orientation that the geometry itself does not have: swapping two of the three inputs flips the sign without changing any of the lengths involved. The factor of one sixth for the tetrahedron then comes from a base-area argument. Use the triangle spanned by the first two vectors as the base: its area is half the parallelogram area, since a triangle on the same two sides is half of it. A pyramid is one third of the prism on the same base, because the cross sections shrink linearly to a point at the apex, so the tetrahedron is one third of one half of the parallelepiped, which is one sixth. Nothing in that reasoning depends on the shape, so the figure of one sixth holds for any three edges, including obtuse and degenerate-looking configurations.

questions.explanation: A model answer should build the volume from a base area and a perpendicular height, then give the sixth as one third of a halved base: a triangle on two of the sides has half the parallelogram area, and a pyramid is one third of the prism on the same base.
questions.hint: Use the triangle half the parallelogram as the base, then a third for the height.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why perspective needs a homogeneous coordinate
questions.learningObjective: justify the use of homogeneous coordinates for perspective
questions.practice: explaining why perspective needs a fourth coordinate
questions.stem: Explain why a single 3 by 3 matrix cannot carry out a perspective projection, and what the extra homogeneous coordinate makes possible.

answer.exemplar: In ordinary coordinates a point on a ray from the eye is not pinned down by its direction alone: the point twice as far along the same ray is a different point in space, and a linear map with no translation has to send multiples of a direction to multiples of the same direction with the multiple forced to be the same for every ray. Perspective does not respect that, because the scale factor along a ray varies with how far the point sits from the eye, and the amount of compression is different in different parts of the image. Three output coordinates cannot carry that extra degree of freedom, so a three by three matrix has no room for it. Adding a fourth coordinate that is free to differ between points breaks the tie: the matrix can now compute a fourth output that records the perspective scale for that point, and the final step divides the first three by it. That division is the projection itself. Because a point and any nonzero multiple of its four-vector describe the same point, the scale stops being a special case, and a translation can be folded into the same matrix by adding a constant to the fourth coordinate. Two properties are worth stating: the same matrix now handles perspective alongside all the parallel projections, and the fourth coordinate is bookkeeping rather than extra geometric information, since it carries no shape of its own.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show that a linear map ties the scale along every ray to one fixed multiple, that perspective needs a scale varying by ray, and that the fourth coordinate together with the final division supplies exactly that variation.
questions.hint: Ask what a point twice as far along a ray has in common with the point at half the distance.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why a plane angle is the complement of the angle between normals
questions.learningObjective: justify the complementary relationship between plane and normal angles
questions.practice: explaining the complement rule for plane angles
questions.stem: Explain why the angle a plane makes with a coordinate plane is the complement of the angle between the two normal vectors.

answer.exemplar: A normal is perpendicular to its own plane, so when one plane is tilted onto the other its normal is carried along by exactly the same tilt, and the target plane's normal has to turn by that same amount in the opposite sense within the plane of tilt. The two normals are therefore left separated by whatever is left of a right angle once the tilt has been subtracted, which is to say the angle between the normals is the complement of the tilt, and the tilt is the angle between the planes. The two limiting cases pin this down. A plane that coincides with the coordinate plane has a normal parallel to the coordinate plane's normal, so the normals meet at angle zero while the planes meet at a right angle. As the plane tips over until it is perpendicular to the coordinate plane, its normal tips over until it lies inside the coordinate plane, where it is a right angle from the coordinate normal and the plane angle has shrunk to zero. The two quantities run in opposite directions and add to a right angle throughout, which is what lets a plane angle be computed from a dot product between normals without ever finding a direction lying in the plane.

questions.explanation: A model answer should use the two limiting cases, a plane coinciding with and a plane perpendicular to the coordinate plane, to pin the relationship down, and should state that the two angles add to a right angle.
questions.hint: Tilt one plane all the way onto the other and watch the two normals tilt with it.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Unit normal first, then a dot product with it
questions.learningObjective: build a unit normal to a plane and use it in a dot product
questions.practice: two-stage normal and dot product
questions.stem: First find a unit normal to the plane through the points (1, 0, 2), (0, 3, -1) and (4, 1, 0). Then report its dot product with the vector (1, 2, -1).

options.misconception: uses only the first component of the normal in the second stage
divides by the squared length of the normal instead of its length
flips the sign of the normal without changing the geometry

questions.explanation: The differences from (1, 0, 2) are (-1, 3, -3) and (3, 1, -2), and their cross product is (-3, -11, -10), so a normal with a positive first entry is (3, 11, 10) with length the square root of 230. The unit normal is that vector over the square root of 230, and dotting it with (1, 2, -1) gives 3 plus 22 minus 10, which is 15, over the square root of 230, that is 0.98907. Dividing by 230 rather than by the square root of 230 is the second-stage slip, and using only the first component of the normal is the first-stage slip.
questions.hint: Take the cross product of two differences from the first point, then normalise.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Unit vector first, then a dot product with it
questions.learningObjective: normalise a vector and then take a dot product with it
questions.practice: two-stage normalisation and dot product
questions.stem: First turn the vector (2, -1, 2) into a unit vector. Then report the dot product of that unit vector with (1, 1, 1).

options.misconception: reports the magnitude from the first stage and never does the second
multiplies the two magnitudes instead of taking a dot product
divides the dot product by three rather than by the magnitude

questions.explanation: The magnitude of (2, -1, 2) is the square root of 4 plus 1 plus 4, which is 3, so the unit vector is (2, -1, 2) over 3. Dotting that with (1, 1, 1) sums the three numerators and divides once by 3, giving 2 minus 1 plus 2 over 3, which is 1. Stopping after the first stage gives 3, and dividing by three a second time would be dividing by the magnitude twice.
questions.hint: Find the magnitude, divide the whole vector by it, then dot with the given vector.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Triple product first, then the tetrahedron volume
questions.learningObjective: compute a scalar triple product and convert it to a tetrahedron volume
questions.practice: two-stage triple product and volume
questions.stem: First compute the scalar triple product of the vectors (1, 2, 3), (4, -5, 6) and (2, 1, 0). Then report the volume of the tetrahedron having those three vectors as the edges from one vertex.

options.misconception: reports the parallelepiped from the first stage and stops there
divides the triple product by three rather than by six
doubles the parallelepiped volume instead of taking a sixth

questions.explanation: The cross product of the first two vectors is (27, 6, -13) and dotting that with (2, 1, 0) gives 54 plus 6, which is 60, and the same 60 comes from the three by three determinant with those rows. The parallelepiped they span is built from six tetrahedra of exactly this shape, so the tetrahedron is 60 over 6, which is 10. Stopping at 60 answers a different question, and dividing by 3 rather than by 6 would count only the corner tetrahedra.
questions.hint: The solid is one sixth of the parallelepiped, not the whole of it.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Intersection point first, then a distance
questions.learningObjective: locate the intersection of two lines and measure it from the origin
questions.practice: two-stage intersection and distance
questions.stem: First find the point where the lines (1, 0, 1) + s(0, 1, -1) and (0, 2, 0) + t(1, 0, -1) meet. Then report the distance from the origin to that point.

options.misconception: reports the squared distance and forgets to take the root
uses only two of the three coordinates of the point
adds the coordinates instead of combining their squares

questions.explanation: Equating the first coordinates forces t to be 1, equating the second then forces s to be 2, and the third coordinates agree at minus 1, so the meeting point is (1, 2, -1). Its distance from the origin is the square root of 1 plus 4 plus 1, which is the square root of 6, giving 2.44949. Reporting 6 forgets the square root, and using only the first two coordinates gives the square root of 2, which is the distance to a different point.
questions.hint: Equate the three coordinates to get both parameters, then take a magnitude.
